coreTruths.title: Every restoration starts a cycle of replacement, so minimally invasive thinking is the antidote to the restorative escalator
coreTruths.broaderContext: Restorative dentistry now leans biological rather than mechanistic. Each restoration begins a cycle of progressively bigger replacements, so the smallest cavity that does the job extends a tooth's lifespan.
coreTruths.body:
## Once a tooth is restored it joins a cycle of replacement

As soon as a restoration goes in, the tooth enters a cycle of replacement. Each subsequent restoration tends to be more destructive than the last. This is the restorative escalator and the patient steps closer to losing the tooth at every cycle [1].

## The price of removing an old restoration is paid in millimetres

Cavity size goes up by about 0.6mm on average every time a restoration is removed [2]. So the question before drilling out a marginal defect is whether it actually needs replacing or whether a repair, polish, or watchful monitoring is the better call.

## Cavity design follows caries and material, not a textbook outline

Cavities should be cut to the biological extent of the caries, the material chosen, and the remaining tooth structure, not to a predetermined classification design [3]. Outline form for resin composite is set by the caries extent. Undercuts are not needed for retention because the bond does the work [4].

## A bigger restoration is not a better restoration

Where amalgam is used, accepted minimal dimensions are 2mm occlusally and 1mm elsewhere [5]. Beyond that, extension is justified only by caries or by the material's needs, not by tradition. Marginal ridges are best left intact where possible to preserve cuspal stiffness [6]. Pre-cementation, the centric stops are marked and preserved on sound tooth or, failing that, kept off the restoration margin itself [7].

citations.quote: As soon as a restoration is placed, there is entry into a 'cycle of replacement' with ever more destructive restorations inevitable over a lifetime. This is sometimes referred to as the 'restorative escalator', with the patient moving closer to losing the tooth with each restoration (however, it should be borne in mind that without appropriate restoration the tooth would be lost much sooner!). A minimally invasive approach wherever possible is, therefore, important in extending the longevity of an individual tooth.
Keep in mind that cavity size is ↑ on average by 0.6mm each time a restoration is removed.
Cavities should not be cut to a predetermined design dictated by a classification but by the biological extent of the caries, the material chosen, and the remaining tooth structure.
Outline form is determined by the extent of the caries and undercuts are not necessary for retention.
Accepted minimal dimensions for amalgam are 2mm occlusally and 1mm elsewhere.
Avoid crossing marginal ridges if possible.
If possible, centric stops should be preserved on sound tooth tissue or the restorative material, but never on the marginal interface of the restoration.

coreTruths.title: A peripheral seal arrests deep caries by starving the bacteria, so pulp exposure is to be avoided rather than chased
coreTruths.broaderContext: Modern deep caries management trades aggressive excavation for a sealed cavity. Pulp preservation depends on starving residual bacteria of substrate, not on removing every last softened fibre.
coreTruths.body:
## Sealed bacteria starve and the lesion arrests

Bacteria sealed under a restoration with a good peripheral seal lose their substrate, the lesion arrests, and the pulpodentinal complex can lay down reparative dentine [1]. That is the whole rationale for selective caries removal — keep the pulp covered, even at the cost of leaving some affected dentine in place.

## Sound dentine is needed at the periphery, but not over the pulp

In smaller lesions with good moisture control, peripheral caries-affected dentine can be left at the ADJ when there are no aesthetic concerns [2]. In larger lesions or when isolation is poor, sound dentine at the ADJ is needed to maximise bond [3]. A small amount of caries-affected dentine can be left over the pulp in a symptomless tooth if a peripheral seal is achievable and pulp exposure is otherwise likely [4].

## Pulp diagnosis decides whether to seal or to extirpate

Management of the deep lesion turns on pulpal status [5]. Reversible pulpitis or healthy pulp gets selective caries removal aimed at preserving vitality. Irreversible pulpitis or necrosis means RCT or extraction. If in doubt, treat as for reversible pulpitis. RCT can always be instituted later, but the patient needs warning that further treatment may follow [6].

## When endodontics is planned the rules flip

Where RCT is the plan, all carious dentine should be removed [7]. The seal logic no longer applies because the pulp is being taken out anyway, and any retained infected dentine sits under the access cavity rather than over a vital pulp.

citations.quote: Bacteria sealed under a restoration that provides a good peripheral seal are denied substrate, therefore lesion arrests. This allows the pulpodentinal complex to lay down reparative dentine.
In smaller lesions with optimal moisture control, some peripheral caries-affected (light brown, sticky, scratchy) dentine can be left at the ADJ provided there are no aesthetic concerns.
In larger lesions or where moisture control is not optimal, then sound dentine at the ADJ is essential to maximize bonding.

A small amount of caries-affected dentine can be left overlying the pulp in a symptomless tooth with an achievable peripheral seal if there is a risk of pulpal exposure (…… Management of the deep carious lesion, p. 249).
Reversible pulpitis/healthy pulp—aim to maintain pulp vitality by selective removal of carious dentine without pulp exposure. See …… Pulp-preserving therapies, p. 334.
If in doubt, treat as for reversible pulpitis. Can always institute RCT later; however, be sure to warn the patient of a possible further need for Rx.
Where endodontics is planned, all carious dentine should be removed.

coreTruths.title: Pulpal pain is diagnosed from the pattern, not from a single test, because the pulp lacks proprioceptive nerves
coreTruths.broaderContext: Toothache diagnosis hinges on history. The pulp can't localise pain, so the response to thermal, percussion and biting tests is read alongside symptom pattern, not as a stand-alone result.
coreTruths.body:
## The pulp cannot localise pain, the periodontal ligament can

The dental pulp has no proprioceptive nerve endings, so a hallmark of pulpal pain is that the patient cannot localise the affected tooth, although the pain does not cross the midline [1]. Once inflammation reaches the periapical tissues, the periodontal ligament's proprioceptive supply takes over and the patient can point straight at the tooth.

## Reversible vs irreversible pulpitis is read from the pattern

Reversible pulpitis is fleeting sharp pain to hot, cold or sweet that subsides as soon as the stimulus is removed. The exam shows an exaggerated response to pulp testing, a carious cavity or leaking restoration, and the tooth is not tender to percussion. Treatment is caries removal and restoration with appropriate pulp protection [2]. Irreversible pulpitis is spontaneous, dull, throbbing pain that lasts minutes to hours, often worse at night, and crucially the pain remains after the stimulus is removed. Heat triggers it and, in later stages, cold may even ease it [3]. Treatment is extirpation and RCT.

## Pulp testing is sensibility, not vitality

The ability of the pulp to recover from injury depends on its blood supply, not on its nerve supply, and that has to be borne in mind when sensibility testing is done [4]. A negative response is one piece of information among many, and an accurate diagnosis of pulpal state on clinical grounds alone is impossible — the only 100% accurate method is histological section [5].

## A few patterns deserve their own labels

Cracked tooth syndrome shows up as sharp pain on biting, often on release of pressure, in a heavily restored tooth, with positive vitality and minimal radiographic signs [6]. Occlusal overload mimics it: pain on biting, sometimes lingering, with mobility, and the differential turns on excursive checks and wear facets [7]. Dentine hypersensitivity is pain to thermal, tactile, or osmotic stimulus from exposed dentine, diagnosed by elimination [8].

citations.quote: The dental pulp does not contain any proprioceptive nerve endings, therefore a characteristic of pulpal pain is that the patient is unable to localize the affected tooth but the pain does not cross the midline.
Fleeting sensitivity/pain to hot, cold, or sweet with immediate onset. Pain is usually sharp and may be difficult to locate. Quickly subsides after removal of the stimulus.

Spontaneous dull, throbbing pain which may last several minutes or hours, be worse at night, and is often pulsatile in nature. Pain exacerbated by hot and cold. In later stages, cold may actually ease symptoms. A characteristic feature is that the pain remains after the removal of the stimulus.

The ability of the pulp to recover from injury depends upon its blood supply, not the nerve supply, which must be borne in mind when vitality (sensibility) testing is carried out (…… Sensibility testing, p. 16).
It is impossible to reliably achieve an accurate ∆ of the state of the pulp on clinical grounds alone; the only 100% accurate method is histological section.

Sharp pain on biting (e.g. cotton-wool roll or a 'Tooth Slooth®')—short duration, pain may cease on release of bite/pressure, and possible cold sensitivity. Some patients find pain elicited on sudden release of bite.
Pain on biting which can be sharp, short duration but can linger as an ache. Often combined with instantaneous hot and cold sensitivity. Tooth may become mobile.

This is pain arising from exposed dentine in response to a thermal, tactile, or osmotic stimulus (not all exposed dentine gives rise to symptoms). It is thought to be due to dentinal fluid movement stimulating pulpal pain receptors.

coreTruths.title: Restorations should be made to fit the existing occlusion, not the other way around
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most restorative work uses the conformative approach: protect the patient's existing occlusion, avoid creating new interferences. Reorganisation is reserved for full-mouth rehabilitation.
coreTruths.body:
## The conformative approach is the default

In most situations restorations are made to conform to the patient's existing occlusion, with the main consideration being to avoid introducing iatrogenic interferences [1]. The reorganised approach, where a new occlusal scheme is established in retruded contact position, is for cases where extensive crown and bridgework would destroy the existing occlusion anyway [2].

## Centric stops are precious — mark them before drilling

Before preparing a tooth, mark the centric stops with articulating paper and try to preserve them, or place the preparation margins past the occlusal contact areas [3]. After restoring, check intercuspal position to ensure the restoration is not high but also that it has recreated the centric stops, because a restoration left out of occlusion will allow over-eruption and that creates new interferences [4].

## Iatrogenic interferences are the practical concern, not pure occlusion theory

Occlusal interferences usually fall within the patient's neuromuscular adaptive capacity and produce subclinical or no dysfunction. That capacity is lowered by stress and emotional factors, so in susceptible patients an iatrogenic interference can trigger muscle hyperactivity [5]. The takeaway is straightforward: do not introduce interferences during restorative procedures.

## Best fit beats wax bites for ICP

A wax squash bite is inaccurate because the mandible can deviate as the teeth bite through the wax. For ICP it is better to use no record at all and mount the models to the position of best fit [6]. When the prepared model no longer fits its opponent, the transfer coping technique with DuraLay is more accurate than another wax bite.

citations.quote: In most situations, restorations are made to conform to the patient's existing occlusion and the main consideration is to prevent the introduction of iatrogenic occlusal interferences. This approach to Rx is known as the conformative approach.

In some circumstances, the conformative approach is not appropriate and a new occlusal scheme must be planned. This is often the case when extensive crown and bridgework is required, such that the patient's existing occlusion will be effectively destroyed by the preparations. A new occlusion is established, free of interferences and with the patient occluding in retruded contact position, which is the only reproducible position.
Before preparing a tooth it is worthwhile marking the centric stops with articulating paper and trying to preserve them if possible.

On completion of the restoration it must be checked in intercuspal position to ensure that it is not high, but also to ensure that it has recreated the centric stops, as if it is out of occlusion then over-eruption will occur (which may produce interferences).

The evidence would suggest that occlusal interferences usually cause either subclinical or no dysfunction because they lie within the adaptive capacity of the patient's neuromusculature. However, this may be lowered by stress and emotional problems so that in susceptible patients occlusal interferences can result in muscle hyperactivity at certain times. It is important therefore to ensure that iatrogenic interferences are not introduced during restorative procedures.

A wax 'squash bite' has commonly been used to record ICP; however, it is inaccurate as the mandible can be deviated as the teeth 'bite' through the wax. For ICP, it is better not to use any record and to mount the models to the position of 'best fit'.

coreTruths.title: Tooth wear is irreversible, multifactorial and only sometimes pathological, so management starts with cause not crowns
coreTruths.broaderContext: Tooth wear blends erosion, attrition, abrasion and possibly abfraction. Some loss is physiological with age. Restorative intervention belongs at the end of a chain that begins with cause control.
coreTruths.body:
## Wear is what's left after caries and trauma are excluded

Tooth wear is the irreversible loss of tooth substance by factors other than trauma or caries, usually a combination of erosion, attrition, abrasion and possibly abfraction [1]. Some loss during life is inevitable. Wear is pathological only when it produces unsatisfactory appearance, sensitivity, loss of vitality, or mechanical problems [2]. Wear that would be normal in a 70-year-old would not be normal in a 20-year-old.

## Erosion has intrinsic and extrinsic patterns worth knowing

Erosion is loss of tooth substance from non-bacterial chemical attack, and once it is through to dentine it accelerates [3]. Intrinsic acid from gastro-oesophageal reflux, vomiting in eating disorders, pregnancy or rumination affects palatal surfaces of upper anteriors and the occlusal/buccal of lower molars, and warrants referral [4]. Extrinsic dietary acid from carbonated drinks and citrus juice classically hits labial surfaces of upper anteriors [5]. Xerostomic patients are at increased risk overall.

## Diagnosis demands a tactful history because the cause may have stopped

Wear may be due to a factor that no longer operates, so the history sometimes has to delve tactfully into the past [6]. Staining of worn surfaces suggests historic or slow wear, sensitivity suggests progression. Monitoring with study models, silicone indices and photos before operative intervention is sensible.

## Management is a chain, not a single restorative leap

Focus is on removal of aetiological factors, prevention, and monitoring [7]. Restorative work is for unsatisfactory appearance, sensitivity, or functional problems. For localised anterior tooth wear the Dahl approach can create space by anterior intrusion and posterior eruption, with composite added palatally to a minimum thickness of 1.5mm. The patient needs warning that posterior teeth will be out of contact for 3–6 months [8]. Predictability of this method decreases with age. Pulpal involvement turns up in 9–12% of tooth wear cases [9].

citations.quote: This is the irreversible loss of tooth substance by factors other than trauma or caries. Usually caused by combinations of erosion, attrition, abrasion, and possibly abfraction.

Some tooth wear during life is inevitable (physiological), but where it has resulted in an unsatisfactory appearance, sensitivity, loss of vitality, or mechanical problems (pathological), the condition warrants investigation and Rx.

Loss of tooth substance from non-bacterial chemical attack. Enamel initially becomes smooth and shiny then eventually dentine is exposed. This leads to cup-shaped lesions on the occlusal and incisal surfaces and proud amalgams. Once erosion is through to dentine it can accelerate.

Acid from stomach due to gastro-oesophageal reflux, vomiting in relation to eating disorder (…… Anorexia nervosa/bulimia nervosa, p. 555), pregnancy, stress, or rumination. Such conditions warrant referral. Affects palatal surfaces of ULS and occlusal/buccal of lower molars.
Dietary (e.g. citric, phosphoric, acetic acid)—found in carbonated drinks, fruit/citrus juices, and pickles. Labial surfaces of ULS teeth classically affected.
As tooth wear may be due to a factor which no longer operates, it may be necessary (tactfully) to delve into the patient's past.
Focus should be on removal of aetiological factors, prevention, and monitoring.

For localized anterior tooth wear, use of the 'Dahl' approach can create space by a combination of anterior tooth intrusion and posterior tooth eruption. Composite is added to the palatal surfaces of the anteriors (minimum thickness 1.5mm palatally). Warn the patient that the posterior teeth will be out of contact but will come together again in 3–6 months.
Sensitivity is a frequent problem in tooth wear. There may be pulpal involvement in 9–12% of cases.

coreTruths.title: Replacing a failed restoration without diagnosing why it failed just sets up the next failure
coreTruths.broaderContext: Restoration failure has identifiable causes — caries, occlusion, technique, materials, patient factors. Repair often beats replacement, and secondary caries diagnosis now leans on observation rather than reflex drilling.
coreTruths.body:
## Identify the cause before reaching for the bur

Before replacing a failed restoration, the cause of failure has to be identified, and the question is whether repair will do the job rather than replacement [1]. Reasons for failure cluster into a familiar list: further caries or fracture, aesthetic deterioration, poor understanding of the occlusion, incorrect preparation, wrong material choice, manipulation errors, and patient factors like bruxism or biting hard objects [2].

## Marginal ditching is not an automatic redo

Marginal integrity fails through creep, corrosion, ditching, shrinkage or chipping [3]. If the patient can keep the margin plaque-free and there is no recurrent caries, replacement may not be needed. Otherwise secondary caries becomes the worry. Secondary caries is hard to diagnose, so careful clinical and radiographic observation now beats reflex intervention [4]. Intervention is justified only when the lesion is in dentine and there is evidence of progression or cavitation.

## Loyalty to one dentist is itself a survival factor

Patients who change dentists frequently are more at risk of replacement restorations than those loyal to one GDP [5]. Each fresh pair of eyes is more likely to call a borderline restoration failed and replace it, paying the 0.6mm tax noted earlier.

## Long-term failure prevention is half technique, half patient education

To prevent secondary caries, both excellent restorative technique and patient education to reduce caries rate are needed [6]. Replacing the restoration without changing the host environment just resets the clock on the same failure.

citations.quote: Before replacing a failed restoration, it is important to identify the cause of failure and decide whether this can be dealt with by repair rather than replacement.
Further caries, tooth fracture, or material fracture.
This can be due to creep/corrosion and ditching of amalgams or shrinkage of composites/GIC or marginal chipping.

If the patient can keep the margin plaque free and there is no recurrent caries then it may not be necessary to replace the restoration. If not, 2° or recurrent caries may be a risk. 2° caries is difficult to diagnose, but careful observation (clinically and radiographically) rather than intervention, is now advocated. Intervention is only indicated when the lesion is in dentine, and there is evidence of progression &/or cavitation is present.
Patients who change dentists frequently are more at risk of replacement restorations than those who are loyal to the same GDP.
To prevent 2° caries it is important not only to educate the patient to reduce their caries rate but also to use an excellent restorative technique to ensure good long term-restorations.

coreTruths.title: Posts retain crowns, they do not reinforce roots, and the ferrule does the structural work
coreTruths.broaderContext: Post and core thinking has moved away from reinforcement myths. Posts transfer load to the root, the ferrule resists fracture, and the post type changes which failures are recoverable.
coreTruths.body:
## Posts are for retention, not reinforcement

Post and cores provide support and retention for a crown but they do not reinforce teeth [1]. They transfer forces to the root. A ferrule effect protects the root from those forces to a degree.

## A post commits the tooth — check the endodontics first

Placing a post makes further orthograde endodontics difficult, so the root-filling and apical condition must be checked before committing. If in doubt, repeat the RCT before placing the post [2]. The minimum apical seal of well-condensed GP to leave behind is 5mm, with the post ideally at least equal to the anticipated crown height [3].

## Parallel-sided beats tapered, serrated beats threaded

Parallel-sided posts are generally preferred to tapered: more retention and less stress within the root canal [4]. Threaded posts retain better than smooth but they generate more stress in the canal and are contraindicated. Serrated posts increase surface area for retention without concentrating stress [5].

## Fibre posts fail in retrievable ways

Fibre posts (ceramic or carbon-fibre reinforced) are more flexible than metal and so less likely to cause root fracture. Failure with fibre posts is most often decementation or secondary caries rather than fracture, which makes the failure more retrievable [6].

## In multirooted teeth the Nayyar core often beats a post

Posterior multirooted teeth need a different approach because the canals diverge. Amalgam packed into the coronal aspect of the root canals (Nayyar/Amalcore technique) and built up as a core is the preferred technique [7]. RMGIC or resin composite work too, with a dentine adhesive system to enhance retention.

citations.quote: Post and cores provide support and retention for a crown but they do not reinforce teeth. They transfer forces to the root of the tooth. A ferrule effect will protect the root from this to an extent.
The placement of a post makes further orthograde endodontics difficult, so it is important to check first that the root-filling and apical condition are satisfactory. If in doubt, repeat RCT.
As a general guide the post should be at least equal to the anticipated crown height, but a minimum of 5mm of well-condensed GP should be left.

Parallel-sided posts are generally preferred to tapered as they provide greater retention and do not generate as much stress within the root canal. Tapered posts, however, are less likely to perforate in the apical region and are better for small tapered roots, e.g. lateral incisors.

Threaded posts provide ↑ retention than smooth-sided; however, they will ↑ stress within the root canal and are therefore C/I. Serrated posts do not concentrate stress but simply ↑ the surface area for retention.

They are more flexible than metal posts and therefore less likely to cause root fracture. Failure with fibre posts is most commonly due to decementation or 2° caries rather than fracture so failure can be more retrievable.

In multirooted teeth there is divergence of the root canals. Preformed posts can be cemented into one or more canals. Amalgam may also be packed into the coronal aspect of the root canals (Amalcore or Nayyar technique) and an amalgam core built up, which is the preferred technique.
